changes.before: Wrap a lazy report in a Suspense boundary and observe pending, ready, and reused states.
changes.after: Show fallback content while React waits for a lazy component to become ready.

before: React.lazy(load) declares a component whose loader runs when React first tries to render it. Declare the lazy component outside App so normal App renders reuse the same declaration.
The loader returns a Promise: an object representing a result that may arrive later. A pending Promise has no result yet. Resolving it supplies a result; rejecting it supplies an error.

For lazy, the resolved result must be an object whose default property contains a component. For example, React.lazy(() => Promise.resolve({ default: Greeting })) makes Greeting the loaded component. Promise.resolve creates an already-resolved Promise, so that small example need not visibly wait.

React caches the loader Promise and its resolved component for that lazy declaration. Hiding and showing it again does not reload the component code. This does not preserve the child's local state after unmounting, and it is not a general data cache.

If loading rejects, the nearest Error Boundary handles the error; Suspense is for waiting, not a replacement for error handling. Ordinary fetching inside useEffect does not automatically activate Suspense.

The supplied Toggle report button shows or hides the child. Finish simulated load settles the Promise. Replace the TODO paragraph with a Suspense boundary whose fallback is

Loading report

, and put inside. role="status" identifies a status message for assistive technology and our check.

In a real bundler-supported app, React.lazy(() => import("./Report.js")) can load a separate module whose default export is the component. That dynamic import is not run by this single-file exercise. Reset the runner to get a fresh pending Promise.
after: `React.lazy` declares a component whose loader runs when React first tries to show it. Declare it outside App so later App renders reuse the same declaration.
A Promise represents a result that may arrive later. Pending means it is still waiting. Resolving supplies the result; rejecting reports a failure.
A lazy loader must return a Promise whose result has a `default` property containing the component. Here, the result will be `{default: Greeting}`.
React remembers the Promise and loaded component for this lazy declaration. Hiding and showing it again does not need to load the code again. Removing a component can still discard its local state.
Suspense handles waiting. If the loader rejects, use an Error Boundary for the failure. Ordinary fetching inside an Effect does not automatically make Suspense show its fallback.

`new Promise` immediately gives its callback a resolve function. This example saves a function that calls resolve later. The button controls when it becomes ready; no network request or download happens.

` as the fallback. Toggle report shows or hides it, and Finish simulated load makes it ready.

before.question: A lazily loaded HelpPanel finishes loading successfully. You hide it, then show it again using the same lazy declaration. What should you expect?
choices: React calls the loader again every time because the panel was hidden.
React reuses the loaded component; its code need not load again.
The panel can never appear again after it has been hidden.
before.explanation: The Promise and loaded component are cached for that lazy declaration. Reusing its code does not guarantee preservation of a previously unmounted component's local state.

after.question: A lazy HelpPanel has loaded. It is hidden and shown again with the same lazy declaration. What happens?
choices: The loader must run again every time.
React reuses the loaded component code.
after.explanation: React keeps the loaded component for that declaration. Keeping its code does not preserve local state after removal.

changes.before: Actual React18.3.1 controlled-Promise fixture. Exercises waiting/reveal/cache semantics, not real network code splitting or React19 APIs. The supplied loader controls are instructional scaffolding.
changes.after: The supplied Promise lets you control the waiting step. This exercise does not download or split a real module.
